title: Polynomial kernels for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
formal:
Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized solely by the deletion budget? More precisely, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(K\), constants \(C,c>0\), and a polynomial \(p\), such that for every finite digraph \(D\) and nonnegative integer \(k\), \(K\) runs in at most \(p(L)\) steps on the explicit input of bit length \(L\), and outputs one instance \((D^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same problem satisfying
\[
D\text{ has a directed feedback vertex set of size at most }k
\iff
D^{\prime}\text{ has one of size at most }k^{\prime},
\]
with the entire output encoding having at most \(C(k+1)^{c}\) bits? The constants and algorithm must work for all inputs. No additional structural parameter or promise on the input or the remaining acyclic graph is permitted.

source_formulation.text: Directed Feedback Vertex Set has a kernel of exponential size \(k O(k)\) , as the problem was shown fixed-parameter tractable by Chen et al. \([4], [\ldots ]\)
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 2

context:
The 2016 source recalls a \(k^{O(k)}\)-size kernel following from fixed-parameter tractability, while explicitly leaving a polynomial-size kernel open. The missing improvement concerns how small a polynomial-time preprocessing can make every instance, rather than whether exponential dependence on the solution budget is possible.

The source proves polynomial kernels when deletion must leave an out-tree, an out-forest, or a directed pumpkin. These are stronger conditions than merely destroying directed cycles, so the results do not constitute a kernel for general Directed Feedback Vertex Set.

The WADS 2019 result, subsequently published in the 2025 journal article, gives a polynomial kernel with parameter \(k+\ell\), where \(\ell\) is the size of a supplied vertex set whose removal leaves an underlying undirected graph of fixed bounded treewidth. Here treewidth at most \(\eta\) means that there are vertex bags indexed by a tree, each of size at most \(\eta+1\), covering all vertices and both endpoints of every edge, with the bags containing each vertex forming a connected subtree. The constant \(\eta\) is fixed. The extra \(\ell\) need not be bounded by a polynomial in \(k\); the general question therefore remains distinct.

The same work distinguishes the combined parameter \(k+\ell\) from parameterization by \(\ell\) alone. Its conditional obstruction for the latter does not rule out a polynomial kernel in the solution budget \(k\).
why: Directed Feedback Vertex Set is a central test of how much efficient preprocessing can compress a fixed-parameter tractable cycle-hitting problem. A polynomial kernel would reduce every large instance with a small deletion budget to a polynomial amount of relevant information. A rigorous obstruction would distinguish directed cycle constraints from many successful kernelization settings.

sentences: Directed Feedback Vertex Set asks whether deleting at most a given number of vertices destroys every directed cycle.
The question is whether polynomial-time preprocessing can always replace an instance by one of size polynomial in that deletion budget.
The replacement must preserve the exact yes or no answer.
Known kernels with extra structural parameters or more restrictive deletion targets do not give this guarantee.
Resolving the general question would clarify the limits of efficient compression for directed cycle problems.

definitions:
A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has a finite explicitly listed vertex set and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc have no effect and need not be represented. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{0},\ldots,v_{r-1}\), with \(r\ge1\), having arcs from each vertex to the next, including from \(v_{r-1}\) to \(v_{0}\). Thus a self-loop is a cycle and two opposite arcs form a cycle.

A directed feedback vertex set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that the induced digraph \(D[V\setminus S]\) has no directed cycle. The decision instance is YES exactly when some such set has \(|S|\le k\). The remaining graph may be any directed acyclic graph, including a disconnected one.

Encode vertices by integers \(1,\ldots,n\), list all vertices and arcs, and encode \(k\) in binary using a fixed ordinary self-delimiting binary encoding. Measure preprocessing time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine in the total input length \(L\). The output uses the same encoding, with newly numbered vertices and a nonnegative binary integer \(k^{\prime}\). Bounding only the number of output vertices while permitting arbitrarily much auxiliary information would not meet the stated size requirement.

A kernel preserves the YES/NO answer, not necessarily the optimum value, the original vertex labels, or every solution. The output budget may differ from the input budget. The requirement is a single small instance of this same unweighted decision problem; a list of oracle queries or a compression into a different language is a different notion.

The preprocessing time must be polynomial in \(L\), uniformly for all \(k\). A procedure taking \(f(k)L^{d}\) time for an unrestricted computable function \(f\) is not by itself a polynomial-time kernelization. The case \(k=0\) is covered by the bound \(C(k+1)^{c}\). Allowing loops makes the model explicit and does not change the question: each loop forces its vertex into any deletion set, while repeated arcs can be removed.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of an algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial preprocessing, exact answer equivalence, and polynomial output bit bound depending only on the original deletion budget, or refute that existence. A conditional lower bound must state its complexity assumption explicitly; it is not an unconditional refutation. A kernel using a larger structural parameter does not settle this target.
